New puzzle structures (a bench with distances, back-to-back rows, a row with ages, a hexagonal table with drinks, a square table with everyone facing the centre, an eight-seat rectangular table, a circle with ages and mixed facing, a ten-seat rectangular table with persons facing across, floors numbered from the top, a ground floor numbered 0, two persons per floor, a building of unknown height, three stacks of boxes, boxes holding counted items, months with colours, appointment dates with weekdays, a two-year month grid, a hobby week, designations with branches). Puzzles are brute-forced for a unique arrangement; syllogisms are checked over every Venn-region model; inequalities over all integer assignments; data sufficiency by enumerating models for each statement subset; blood relations, directions, coding (inferred rules checked against alternative simple rules), series, alphabet, ranking and input-output are recomputed in code. Verbal-reasoning items are hand-written. All questions await human review.

stimuli.title: Six persons in a row, with favourite fruits
stimuli.content:
Six persons Ishan, Jhanvi, Kabir, Lavanya, Moksh and Nysa sit in a straight row, all facing north. Each of them likes a different fruit among Apple, Banana, Cherry, Guava, Kiwi and Mango. (Facing north, a person's right is towards the east end of the row.)

- Kabir sits at the extreme right end of the row.
- Nysa sits third to the left of Kabir.
- The person who likes Guava sits immediately to the right of Nysa.
- Only one person sits between Ishan and the person who likes Guava.
- Lavanya likes Guava, and Ishan likes Mango.
- Moksh is not an immediate neighbour of Ishan.
- The person who likes Cherry sits immediately to the left of the person who likes Apple.
- Jhanvi does not like Banana.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Number the seats 1 to 6 from the left. Kabir = 6, so Nysa (third to his left) = 3.
Step 2: The Guava-lover sits at seat 4, and Lavanya likes Guava, so Lavanya = 4.
Step 3: Ishan is two seats from seat 4: seat 2 or seat 6; seat 6 is Kabir's, so Ishan = 2.
Step 4: Seats 1 and 5 are left for Jhanvi and Moksh. Moksh cannot sit next to Ishan, so Moksh = 5 and Jhanvi = 1.
Step 5: Ishan likes Mango. Cherry is immediately left of Apple; among the free seats 1, 3, 5, 6 the only adjacent pair is 5–6, so Moksh likes Cherry and Kabir Apple.
Step 6: Jhanvi and Nysa share Banana and Kiwi; Jhanvi does not like Banana, so Jhanvi likes Kiwi and Nysa Banana.

| Seat (from the left) | Person | Fruit |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Jhanvi | Kiwi |
| 2 | Ishan | Mango |
| 3 | Nysa | Banana |
| 4 | Lavanya | Guava |
| 5 | Moksh | Cherry |
| 6 | Kabir | Apple |

stimuli.title: Eight teachers in two facing rows
stimuli.content:
Eight teachers Farid, Gitali, Hemant, Inaya, Jyotsna, Kartik, Lalima and Mitul sit in two parallel rows of four seats each. The persons in Row 1 face south and the persons in Row 2 face north, so each person in one row faces exactly one person in the other row. Each of them teaches a different subject among Biology, Chemistry, Economics, English, Geography, History, Maths and Physics.

- Gitali sits at an extreme end of Row 1.
- Kartik faces Gitali.
- Inaya sits second to the right of Kartik.
- Mitul sits immediately to the left of Inaya.
- Farid faces Mitul.
- The person who teaches History sits immediately to the left of Farid.
- Hemant teaches Physics and sits in Row 1.
- Jyotsna does not sit at an end of a row.
- The person who teaches Maths faces the person who teaches History.
- Lalima teaches Economics.
- Gitali teaches English, and the person who teaches Geography sits immediately to the left of Gitali.
- Kartik does not teach Biology.
stimuli.solution:
Number the seats 1 to 4 from west to east in both rows. For Row 1 (facing south) the right is west; for Row 2 (facing north) the right is east.
Step 1: Gitali is at an end of Row 1 and Kartik faces her. Inaya is second to Kartik's right (east), so Kartik must be at seat 1 (from seat 4 there is no room): Gitali = Row 1 seat 1, Kartik = Row 2 seat 1, Inaya = Row 2 seat 3.
Step 2: Mitul is immediately to Inaya's left (west): Row 2 seat 2. Farid faces him: Row 1 seat 2.
Step 3: Farid faces south, so his left is east: the History teacher sits at Row 1 seat 3. Jyotsna sits in a middle seat, and the only free middle seat is Row 1 seat 3, so Jyotsna teaches History. The Maths teacher faces her: Inaya.
Step 4: Hemant is in Row 1, so he takes Row 1 seat 4; Lalima takes Row 2 seat 4.
Step 5: Gitali teaches English; immediately to her left (east) is Farid: Geography. Hemant Physics, Lalima Economics. Kartik and Mitul share Biology and Chemistry; Kartik is not the Biology teacher, so Kartik teaches Chemistry and Mitul Biology.

| Seat | Row 1 (facing south) | Row 2 (facing north) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Gitali – English | Kartik – Chemistry |
| 2 | Farid – Geography | Mitul – Biology |
| 3 | Jyotsna – History | Inaya – Maths |
| 4 | Hemant – Physics | Lalima – Economics |

stimuli.title: Seven persons on nine seats, facing north or south
stimuli.content:
Nine seats are placed in a straight row, numbered 1 to 9 from the west end. Seven persons Jivika, Kanav, Mehak, Oindri, Pushkar, Riyansh and Sahana sit on seven of them, so two seats are vacant. Some of the persons face north and the others face south. (Facing north, the right is east; facing south, the right is west.) A vacant seat is counted as a seat but not as a person.

- Pushkar sits in the middle seat of the row and faces south.
- Jivika sits immediately to the left of Pushkar.
- Kanav sits second to the right of Pushkar.
- Kanav and Jivika face opposite directions.
- Sahana sits immediately to the right of Kanav.
- Mehak faces north and sits second to the left of Sahana.
- Riyansh sits at an extreme end of the row and faces the same direction as Mehak.
- Oindri sits immediately to the left of Riyansh.
- Oindri and Sahana face the same direction.
- Exactly four persons face south.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Pushkar = seat 5, facing south, so his right is west and his left is east. Jivika (immediately to his left) = 6 and Kanav (second to his right) = 3.
Step 2: Riyansh faces north (like Mehak) and Oindri sits immediately to his left (west), so Riyansh cannot be at seat 1: Riyansh = 9 and Oindri = 8.
Step 3: Suppose Kanav faced north. Then Jivika faces south, Sahana = 4, and Sahana must face north (facing south, the seat second to her left would be Jivika's seat 6), so Mehak = 2; Oindri faces north like Sahana. Only Pushkar and Jivika would face south, not four: rejected.
Step 4: So Kanav faces south and Jivika north. Sahana = 2 (Kanav's right is west). Facing north, the seat second to Sahana's left would be seat 0, so Sahana faces south and Mehak = 4. Oindri faces south like Sahana. South-facing: Pushkar, Kanav, Sahana, Oindri (four). Seats 1 and 7 are vacant.

| Seat | Person | Faces |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | vacant | — |
| 2 | Sahana | south |
| 3 | Kanav | south |
| 4 | Mehak | north |
| 5 | Pushkar | south |
| 6 | Jivika | north |
| 7 | vacant | — |
| 8 | Oindri | south |
| 9 | Riyansh | north |

stimuli.title: Eight persons facing away from a round table, with flowers
stimuli.content:
Eight persons Ishwar, Jasmin, Lavina, Naren, Prisha, Reyansh, Udita and Vaibhav sit around a circular table, equally spaced, all facing away from the centre. Each likes a different flower among Daisy, Iris, Lily, Lotus, Marigold, Orchid, Rose and Tulip. (Facing outside, a person's right is clockwise and the left is anticlockwise.)

- Naren sits third to the right of Ishwar.
- Udita sits opposite Naren.
- Prisha sits immediately to the right of Ishwar.
- Only two persons sit between Reyansh and Prisha, and Reyansh is not an immediate neighbour of Naren.
- Jasmin sits second to the left of Vaibhav.
- The person who likes Lotus sits opposite Ishwar, and Lavina likes Rose.
- The person who likes Orchid sits immediately to the right of the person who likes Rose.
- Udita likes Tulip, and the person who likes Daisy sits second to the right of Udita.
- Ishwar likes neither Iris nor Lily, and Naren does not like Lily.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Fix Ishwar. Counting clockwise (to his right): Prisha is 1st, Naren 3rd. Udita is opposite Naren, i.e. immediately to Ishwar's left.
Step 2: Two persons between Reyansh and Prisha puts Reyansh 3 places from Prisha: either next to Naren (not allowed) or two places to Ishwar's left, beyond Udita. So, going anticlockwise from Ishwar: Udita, Reyansh, then two free seats, then Naren.
Step 3: The free seats are the two between Reyansh and Naren and the one between Naren and Prisha. Jasmin is second to Vaibhav's left (two places anticlockwise): only Vaibhav next to Naren on the Reyansh side with Jasmin next to Naren on the Prisha side fits. Lavina takes the seat next to Reyansh.
Step 4: Lotus is opposite Ishwar: Vaibhav. Lavina likes Rose and the person to her right (clockwise) likes Orchid: Reyansh. Udita likes Tulip; second to her right (clockwise) is Prisha: Daisy. Iris, Lily and Marigold remain for Ishwar, Naren and Jasmin: Ishwar Marigold, Naren Iris, Jasmin Lily.

| Seat (anticlockwise from Ishwar) | Person | Flower |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Ishwar | Marigold |
| 1 | Udita | Tulip |
| 2 | Reyansh | Orchid |
| 3 | Lavina | Rose |
| 4 | Vaibhav | Lotus |
| 5 | Naren | Iris |
| 6 | Jasmin | Lily |
| 7 | Prisha | Daisy |

stimuli.title: Seven floors and seven instruments
stimuli.content:
Seven persons Aarohi, Faisal, Hemal, Ilesh, Jagat, Keya and Mridula live on the seven floors of a building, one on each floor. The lowermost floor is floor 1 and the topmost floor 7. Each of them plays a different instrument among Drum, Flute, Guitar, Harmonium, Piano, Sitar and Violin.

- Jagat lives on floor 5 and plays the Guitar.
- Only two persons live between Jagat and the person who plays the Sitar.
- Keya plays the Sitar, and Faisal lives immediately above Keya.
- Hemal plays the Flute and lives on the topmost floor.
- Mridula lives on an odd-numbered floor below Jagat's floor.
- Aarohi does not live on floor 4.
- The person who plays the Piano lives immediately below the person who plays the Violin.
- Mridula does not play the Drum.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Jagat = 5 (Guitar) and Hemal = 7 (Flute). Keya plays the Sitar and lives three floors from Jagat: floor 2 (floor 8 does not exist). Faisal = 3.
Step 2: Mridula lives on an odd floor below 5: floor 1 or 3; 3 is Faisal's, so Mridula = 1. Floors 4 and 6 remain for Aarohi and Ilesh; Aarohi is not on 4, so Aarohi = 6 and Ilesh = 4.
Step 3: Piano is immediately below Violin. The free instruments are Drum, Harmonium, Piano and Violin for floors 1, 3, 4 and 6; the only consecutive pair is 3–4, so Faisal plays the Piano and Ilesh the Violin.
Step 4: Mridula does not play the Drum, so she plays the Harmonium and Aarohi the Drum.

| Floor | Person | Instrument |
|---|---|---|
| 7 | Hemal | Flute |
| 6 | Aarohi | Drum |
| 5 | Jagat | Guitar |
| 4 | Ilesh | Violin |
| 3 | Faisal | Piano |
| 2 | Keya | Sitar |
| 1 | Mridula | Harmonium |

stimuli.title: Eight floors, six residents, two empty floors
stimuli.content:
A building has eight floors, numbered 1 (lowermost) to 8 (topmost). Six persons Hrishi, Jaspreet, Kusum, Prabhat, Sanober and Zara live in it, one person per floor, so two floors are vacant. Each person is from a different city among Bhopal, Cuttack, Jammu, Madurai, Shillong and Udaipur.

- Neither the topmost floor nor the lowermost floor is vacant, and exactly two floors lie between the two vacant floors.
- Hrishi lives on an even-numbered floor, and the floor immediately below his floor is vacant.
- Sanober lives immediately above Hrishi.
- Kusum lives on the lowermost floor and is from Madurai.
- The person from Jammu lives immediately above a vacant floor.
- Zara lives immediately above the person from Jammu.
- Jaspreet lives on the topmost floor.
- Hrishi is from Bhopal, and the person from Udaipur lives immediately above him.
- Zara is not from Cuttack.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Kusum = 1 and Jaspreet = 8. The vacant floors are three apart (two floors between them) and neither is floor 1 or 8: (2, 5), (3, 6) or (4, 7).
Step 2: Hrishi is on an even floor with a vacant floor just below, and Sanober is just above him. (2, 5): Hrishi 6, Sanober 7. (3, 6): Hrishi 4, Sanober 5. (4, 7): Hrishi would be 8, Jaspreet's floor; rejected.
Step 3: Jammu is immediately above a vacant floor and Zara immediately above the Jammu person. Hrishi is from Bhopal, so Jammu cannot be on Hrishi's floor. Case (3, 6): Jammu = 7 and Zara = 8, Jaspreet's floor: rejected. Case (2, 5): Jammu = 3 and Zara = 4 (Jammu on 6 is Hrishi).
Step 4: Floors 3 and 4 hold the Jammu person and Zara, so Prabhat (the only person left) = 3, from Jammu.
Step 5: Udaipur is immediately above Hrishi: Sanober. Zara and Jaspreet share Cuttack and Shillong; Zara is not from Cuttack, so Zara is from Shillong and Jaspreet from Cuttack.

| Floor | Person | City |
|---|---|---|
| 8 | Jaspreet | Cuttack |
| 7 | Sanober | Udaipur |
| 6 | Hrishi | Bhopal |
| 5 | vacant | — |
| 4 | Zara | Shillong |
| 3 | Prabhat | Jammu |
| 2 | vacant | — |
| 1 | Kusum | Madurai |

stimuli.title: Two towers of four floors, with professions
stimuli.content:
Two towers, A and B, stand side by side; each has four floors, numbered 1 (lowermost) to 4 (topmost), with one flat per floor. Eight persons Abhinav, Bansuri, Chiranjeev, Devika, Girija, Mukul, Noor and Pragya live in these eight flats, one in each. Each has a different profession among Architect, Banker, Chef, Dentist, Editor, Florist, Judge and Pilot. 'Directly above/below' means in the same tower.

- Devika lives on the topmost floor of Tower B.
- Abhinav lives in Tower A, one floor below Devika's floor.
- Pragya lives on the same floor as Abhinav, in the other tower.
- Mukul lives directly below Pragya.
- Girija lives in the same tower as Abhinav, on an even-numbered floor.
- Noor lives in the same tower as Girija, on a floor above Girija's.
- Bansuri does not live in Tower B.
- Pragya is the Banker, and the Chef lives directly above the Banker.
- The Judge lives on the same floor as the Chef, and the Pilot lives directly below the Judge.
- The Dentist lives in Tower B, but Mukul is not the Dentist.
- The Florist lives on floor 1, and Girija is not the Architect.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Devika = B4, Abhinav = A3, Pragya = B3 (same floor, other tower) and Mukul = B2.
Step 2: Girija is in Tower A on an even floor: A2 or A4. Noor is above Girija in Tower A, so Girija cannot be on A4: Girija = A2 and Noor = A4 (A3 is Abhinav's).
Step 3: Bansuri is in Tower A, so Bansuri = A1 and Chiranjeev = B1.
Step 4: Pragya (B3) is the Banker, so the Chef is Devika (B4). The Judge is on floor 4 in the other tower: Noor. The Pilot is directly below the Judge: Abhinav.
Step 5: The Dentist is in Tower B but is not Mukul: Chiranjeev. The Florist is on floor 1: Bansuri. Girija and Mukul share Architect and Editor; Girija is not the Architect, so she is the Editor and Mukul the Architect.

| Floor | Tower A | Tower B |
|---|---|---|
| 4 | Noor – Judge | Devika – Chef |
| 3 | Abhinav – Pilot | Pragya – Banker |
| 2 | Girija – Editor | Mukul – Architect |
| 1 | Bansuri – Florist | Chiranjeev – Dentist |

stimuli.title: Eight boxes in a stack, with their contents
stimuli.content:
Eight boxes C, F, H, K, M, R, V and Y are kept one above another in a single stack (position 1 is the bottom and 8 the top). Each box contains different items among Books, Cups, Files, Lamps, Pens, Shoes, Toys and Watches.

- Box V is kept fourth from the bottom.
- Only three boxes are kept between box V and the box containing Toys, and box R contains Toys.
- Box C is kept immediately above box V, and the box containing Pens is kept immediately above box C.
- Box Y contains Pens, and box H is kept above box Y.
- Box F is kept at the bottom of the stack.
- Box K contains Watches, and box M is kept immediately below box K.
- The box containing Lamps is kept immediately below the box containing Books.
- Box H contains Cups, and box M does not contain Books.
- The box containing Shoes is kept at an odd-numbered position.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: V = 4. Toys are four positions from V: position 8 (position 0 does not exist), in box R.
Step 2: C = 5 and the Pens box = 6; Y holds Pens, so Y = 6, and H (above Y) = 7. F = 1.
Step 3: Positions 2 and 3 remain for K and M. M is immediately below K, so M = 2 and K = 3; K holds Watches.
Step 4: H holds Cups. Books, Files, Lamps and Shoes remain for F (1), M (2), V (4) and C (5). Lamps is immediately below Books: V–C (4–5) or F–M (1–2). F–M would give M the Books, which is not allowed, so V holds Lamps and C Books.
Step 5: Shoes is at an odd position: F (1); M holds Files.

| Position | Box | Contents |
|---|---|---|
| 8 | R | Toys |
| 7 | H | Cups |
| 6 | Y | Pens |
| 5 | C | Books |
| 4 | V | Lamps |
| 3 | K | Watches |
| 2 | M | Files |
| 1 | F | Shoes |

stimuli.title: Six coloured boxes in a three-shelf cupboard
stimuli.content:
A cupboard has three shelves: top, middle and bottom. Each shelf holds two boxes, one on the left side and one on the right side, so the left boxes are directly above one another, and so are the right boxes. Six boxes B, D, G, J, L and P are kept in the cupboard, each of a different colour among Black, Green, Orange, Purple, White and Yellow.

- Box D is on the top shelf, on the right side, and it is White.
- Box B is directly below box D.
- Box L is on the same shelf as box D.
- The Yellow box is on the same shelf as box B.
- Box J is not on the middle shelf, and box G is on the right side.
- The Black box is directly above the Orange box.
- The Green box is directly above the Yellow box.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: D = top-right (White), B = middle-right, L = top-left.
Step 2: The free places are middle-left, bottom-left and bottom-right. G is on the right: bottom-right. J is not on the middle shelf: bottom-left. P takes middle-left.
Step 3: The Yellow box shares B's shelf: P (middle-left). The Green box is directly above it: L.
Step 4: Black is directly above Orange. The colours left are Black, Orange and Purple for B (middle-right), G (bottom-right) and J (bottom-left); the only vertical pair is B above G, so B is Black, G Orange and J Purple.

| Shelf | Left | Right |
|---|---|---|
| top | L – Green | D – White |
| middle | P – Yellow | B – Black |
| bottom | J – Purple | G – Orange |

stimuli.title: Eight visits on nine possible dates
stimuli.content:
Eight persons Aryan, Falgun, Ojal, Prem, Rinki, Smita, Tulsi and Varun each visit a museum once. The museum takes visitors only on the 7th, 15th and 23rd of May, June and July of the same year, so there are nine possible dates. Each person visits on a different date, so one of the nine dates has no visitor. 'Between' counts persons, not dates.

- Prem's visit is on 15 June.
- Smita visits in July, and exactly two persons visit between Prem and Smita.
- Falgun visits on the 23rd of a month, after Smita.
- Ojal visits on the date immediately before Smita's date in the list of nine.
- Rinki visits on the 7th of a month that has 30 days.
- Varun visits on the date immediately after Prem's date.
- Aryan visits on the 15th of a month, and Tulsi visits before Aryan.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Prem = 15 June and Varun = 23 June.
Step 2: Smita visits in July with exactly two persons between her and Prem. After Prem come Varun (23 June) and then the July dates; Smita on 15 July puts Varun and the 7 July visitor between them. Smita on 7 July would leave one person between; Smita on 23 July would leave no date for Falgun after her. So Smita = 15 July, Ojal = 7 July and Falgun = 23 July.
Step 3: Rinki is on the 7th of a 30-day month: June (May and July have 31 days), so Rinki = 7 June.
Step 4: The May dates remain for Aryan, Tulsi and the empty date. Aryan is on the 15th: 15 May. Tulsi is before him: 7 May. Nobody visits on 23 May.

| Date | Visitor |
|---|---|
| 7 May | Tulsi |
| 15 May | Aryan |
| 23 May | — |
| 7 June | Rinki |
| 15 June | Prem |
| 23 June | Varun |
| 7 July | Ojal |
| 15 July | Smita |
| 23 July | Falgun |

stimuli.title: Holidays on first Mondays of 2026
stimuli.content:
Six employees Ankit, Gopi, Kanchan, Manas, Rachit and Vrinda each take one day off in 2026. Each takes the first Monday of a different month among February, March, April, May, June and July. 1 January 2026 is a Thursday.

- Ankit's holiday falls on the 1st of its month.
- Rachit's holiday is in the month immediately after Ankit's month.
- Gopi's and Kanchan's holidays both fall on the 2nd of their months, and Gopi's month comes before Kanchan's.
- Manas's holiday falls on an earlier date of its month than Vrinda's holiday does.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Find the first Monday of each month. 1 January is a Thursday, so 1 February (31 days later, 31 = 4 weeks + 3 days) is a Sunday; 1 March (28 days later) is also a Sunday; 1 April is a Wednesday; 1 May a Friday; 1 June a Monday; 1 July a Wednesday. First Mondays: 2 February, 2 March, 6 April, 4 May, 1 June and 6 July.
Step 2: Only June's first Monday is on the 1st, so Ankit = June and Rachit = July.
Step 3: The 2nd occurs in February and March: Gopi = February, Kanchan = March.
Step 4: April (6th) and May (4th) remain; Manas's date is earlier, so Manas = May and Vrinda = April.

| Employee | Month | Date of holiday |
|---|---|---|
| Gopi | February | 2 February 2026 |
| Kanchan | March | 2 March 2026 |
| Vrinda | April | 6 April 2026 |
| Manas | May | 4 May 2026 |
| Ankit | June | 1 June 2026 |
| Rachit | July | 6 July 2026 |

stimuli.title: Six friends and their stamp collections
stimuli.content:
Six friends Ela, Gaurik, Indrani, Kush, Pari and Sohail have collected different numbers of stamps.

- Pari has 42 stamps, which is 9 more than Kush has.
- Gaurik has 6 stamps fewer than Kush.
- Sohail has 60 stamps.
- Indrani's number of stamps is exactly midway between Pari's and Sohail's.
- Ela has the fewest stamps, 18.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Kush = 42 − 9 = 33; Gaurik = 33 − 6 = 27.
Step 2: Indrani = (42 + 60) ÷ 2 = 51.
Step 3: Order from most to fewest: Sohail 60, Indrani 51, Pari 42, Kush 33, Gaurik 27, Ela 18.

stimuli.title: A week of cooks and dishes
stimuli.content:
Seven persons Aakriti, Devesh, Gulnaz, Ishir, Kamya, Lakshit and Mohini each cook a meal at a community kitchen on a different day of the same week, from Monday to Sunday. Each cooks a different dish among Biryani, Dosa, Idli, Khichdi, Paratha, Poha and Upma.

- Aakriti cooks on Thursday, and she cooks Biryani.
- Only two persons cook between Aakriti and the person who cooks Poha.
- Ishir cooks Poha, on a day before Aakriti's day.
- Kamya cooks on the day immediately after Devesh, and Devesh cooks on neither Tuesday nor Friday.
- Lakshit cooks on a day after Aakriti's day, and Gulnaz cooks on a day before Mohini's day.
- Kamya cooks Khichdi, and the person who cooks Paratha cooks on Saturday.
- The person who cooks Dosa cooks on the day immediately before the person who cooks Upma.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Aakriti = Thursday (Biryani). Poha is three days away: Monday or Sunday; Ishir cooks Poha before Thursday, so Ishir = Monday.
Step 2: Devesh and Kamya are on consecutive days. The free days are Tuesday, Wednesday, Friday, Saturday and Sunday, so the pair is Tue–Wed, Fri–Sat or Sat–Sun; Devesh is on neither Tuesday nor Friday, so Devesh = Saturday and Kamya = Sunday.
Step 3: Tuesday, Wednesday and Friday remain. Lakshit is after Thursday: Friday. Gulnaz is before Mohini: Gulnaz Tuesday, Mohini Wednesday.
Step 4: Kamya cooks Khichdi and Devesh (Saturday) Paratha. Dosa, Idli and Upma remain for Gulnaz (Tue), Mohini (Wed) and Lakshit (Fri); Dosa is the day before Upma, so Gulnaz Dosa, Mohini Upma and Lakshit Idli.

| Day | Cook | Dish |
|---|---|---|
| Monday | Ishir | Poha |
| Tuesday | Gulnaz | Dosa |
| Wednesday | Mohini | Upma |
| Thursday | Aakriti | Biryani |
| Friday | Lakshit | Idli |
| Saturday | Devesh | Paratha |
| Sunday | Kamya | Khichdi |

stimuli.title: Five worded inequality symbols
stimuli.content:
In the following question, the symbols ☼, ♪, ☾, ♫ and ✿ are used with these meanings:
'A ☼ B' means 'A is greater than B'; 'A ♪ B' means 'A is less than B'; 'A ☾ B' means 'A is equal to B'; 'A ♫ B' means 'A is not less than B'; 'A ✿ B' means 'A is not greater than B'.
Assuming the statements to be true, find which of the conclusions I and II is/are definitely true.
stimuli.solution: Decode: ☼ means >, ♪ means <, ☾ means =, ♫ means ≥ and ✿ means ≤. Rewrite every statement with the ordinary signs, join them into one chain, and test each conclusion along the chain.

stimuli.title: A three-generation family with a son-in-law
stimuli.content:
A family has eight members: Kunal, Raghav, Ria, Sushila, Tarun, Uma, Vimla and Yash. There are three married couples.

- Raghav and Sushila are married to each other and have exactly two children, Tarun and Uma.
- Vimla is Tarun's wife, and Kunal is their only child.
- Yash is the son-in-law of Raghav.
- Ria is the daughter of Yash.
- Kunal and Ria are the only grandchildren of Sushila.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Raghav's children are Tarun and Uma. A son-in-law is the husband of one's daughter, and Raghav's only daughter is Uma, so Yash is Uma's husband.
Step 2: Ria is Yash's daughter and a grandchild of Sushila, so her mother is Uma.
Step 3: Tree: Raghav + Sushila → Tarun (+ Vimla) → Kunal; Uma (+ Yash) → Ria. Females: Sushila, Uma, Vimla and Ria.

stimuli.title: Machine: digit sums to the left, words to the right

Step II: 85 66 47 lily aster 31 daisy 19 rose tulip
Step III: 85 66 47 aster 31 daisy 19 lily rose tulip
Step IV: 85 66 47 19 aster 31 daisy lily rose tulip

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability

Seven persons Anshul, Bipasha, Chaitanya, Dimple, Eshaan, Fatima and Govind sit in a straight row, all facing south.

- Eshaan sits at the extreme left end of the row.
- Bipasha is not an immediate neighbour of Dimple.

solution.concept: Facing south: the right is towards the west
solution.explanation: Number the seats 1 to 7 from the west end. A person facing south has the west on the right and the east on the left. Dimple = 4, so Fatima (second to her right) = 2. Govind is three seats from Fatima, at 5 (seat −1 does not exist). Chaitanya is immediately to Govind's left: 6. Eshaan is at the left (east) end: 7. Seats 1 and 3 remain; seat 3 is next to Dimple, so Bipasha = 1 and Anshul = 3. The person immediately to Govind's left is Chaitanya (6); third to Chaitanya's right is seat 3: Anshul.
steps: Facing south: right = west (towards seat 1), left = east
Dimple 4 ⇒ Fatima 2 ⇒ Govind 5 ⇒ Chaitanya 6
Eshaan at the left end = seat 7
Bipasha not next to Dimple ⇒ Bipasha 1, Anshul 3
Immediately left of Govind = Chaitanya (6); 6 − 3 = seat 3 ⇒ Anshul
solution.why_others_wrong: Fatima is fourth to Chaitanya's right; Dimple is second; Bipasha is fifth. Reading 'right' as east (as if the row faced north) leads to the wrong seats.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability

Eight persons Lalit, Mansi, Neel, Omkar, Qadir, Rhea, Sonia and Trisha sit in a straight row, all facing north.

- Only three persons sit between Rhea and Omkar.

- Sonia sits immediately to the left of Qadir.
- Qadir is not an immediate neighbour of Omkar.
- Trisha sits second to the right of Mansi.

solution.concept: Testing both cases of a pair clue
solution.explanation: Rhea = seat 3, so Omkar (four seats away) = 7 and Neel = 8. Sonia sits immediately to Qadir's left, so the pair takes seats (1, 2), (4, 5) or (5, 6); (5, 6) puts Qadir next to Omkar. With Sonia 4 and Qadir 5, the free seats 1, 2 and 6 contain no seat that is two places to the right of another, so Trisha and Mansi cannot be placed. Hence Sonia = 1, Qadir = 2, and in seats 4, 5, 6: Mansi 4, Lalit 5, Trisha 6. Midway between Qadir (2) and Neel (8) is seat 5: Lalit.
steps: Rhea 3 ⇒ Omkar 7 (3 − 4 is off the row), Neel 8
Sonia–Qadir pair: (1, 2), (4, 5) or (5, 6); (5, 6) puts Qadir next to Omkar
Pair (4, 5) leaves seats 1, 2, 6: no 'Mansi + 2' fits ⇒ Sonia 1, Qadir 2
Free seats 4, 5, 6 ⇒ Mansi 4, Lalit 5, Trisha 6
Midway between 2 and 8 = seat 5 ⇒ Lalit
solution.why_others_wrong: Mansi (4) and Trisha (6) are one seat off the midpoint; Rhea sits next to Qadir.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Some persons sit in a straight row, all facing north. The number of persons is not given.

- Tanuj sits fourth to the right of Sneha.

Sneha = 6 + 3 = 9th; Tanuj = 9 + 4 = 13th from the left
Right of Tanuj = 5 ⇒ total = 13 + 5 = 18

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Six persons Arpit, Bhavya, Devansh, Hiya, Kiaan and Myra sit in a straight row, all facing north. Each holds a card with a different number among 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 and 13.
- The person holding card 13 sits at an extreme end of the row.
- Hiya holds card 7 and sits third to the left of the person holding card 13.
- The card numbers of Hiya's two immediate neighbours add up to 12.
- Kiaan sits immediately to the right of Hiya and holds a smaller number than Hiya.
- Myra sits at an extreme end and holds card 11.
- Arpit's card number is 4 more than Devansh's.
- Devansh does not sit next to Kiaan.

What is the sum of the card numbers of Bhavya and the person who sits third to the left of Bhavya?

solution.concept: Seating combined with number arithmetic
solution.explanation: Myra (11) and the holder of 13 take the two ends. Hiya is three seats to the left of the 13-holder, so the 13 is at the right end (seat 6), Hiya = 3 and Myra = 1. Kiaan = 4 with a card smaller than 7: 3 or 5. Hiya's neighbours (seats 2 and 4) add up to 12, so seat 2 holds 9 (with Kiaan 3); with Kiaan 5, seat 2 would need 7, Hiya's own card. Cards 5 and 13 remain. Arpit = Devansh + 4 allows Arpit 13 / Devansh 9 or Arpit 9 / Devansh 5; the second puts Devansh at seat 5, next to Kiaan, so Devansh = seat 2 (9), Arpit = seat 6 (13) and Bhavya = seat 5 (5). Third to Bhavya's left is seat 2, Devansh (9): 5 + 9 = 14.
steps: 13 at an end with Hiya three seats to its left ⇒ 13 at seat 6, Hiya 3, Myra 1
Kiaan 4 with 3 or 5; seat 2 + seat 4 = 12 ⇒ Kiaan 3, seat 2 = 9
Cards 5 and 13 left; Devansh not beside Kiaan ⇒ Devansh 2 (9), Arpit 6 (13), Bhavya 5 (5)
Third to the left of Bhavya (5) = seat 2 = Devansh (9); 5 + 9 = 14
solution.why_others_wrong: 12 adds Kiaan's and Devansh's cards; 16 and 18 use Hiya's or Arpit's card in place of Bhavya's or Devansh's.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Some persons sit in a straight row, all facing north. The number of persons is not given; Kavish, Laila, Mohan, Nidhi and Ojas are among them.
- Kavish sits seventh from the left end.
- Exactly five persons sit between Kavish and Laila.
- Mohan sits third to the right of Laila.
- Only two persons sit between Mohan and Kavish.
- Nidhi sits sixth to the right of Kavish and is fourth from the right end.
- Ojas sits exactly midway between Mohan and the person at the right end of the row.

How many persons sit between Laila and Ojas?

solution.concept: Resolving a two-sided clue with a second clue
solution.explanation: Kavish is 7th from the left, so Laila (six places away) is 1st or 13th. Mohan is three places to Laila's right (4th or 16th) and three places from Kavish (4th or 10th): only 4th fits both, so Laila = 1st and Mohan = 4th. Nidhi = 7 + 6 = 13th and is 4th from the right, so the row has 13 + 3 = 16 persons. Ojas is midway between Mohan (4th) and the right end (16th): (4 + 16) ÷ 2 = 10th. Between Laila (1st) and Ojas (10th) sit 8 persons.
steps: Laila = 7 ± 6 ⇒ 1st or 13th
Mohan = Laila + 3 ∈ {4, 16} and Kavish ± 3 ∈ {4, 10} ⇒ Mohan 4th, Laila 1st
Nidhi = 13th and 4th from the right ⇒ 16 persons
Between 1st and 10th: 10 − 1 − 1 = 8
solution.why_others_wrong: Seven and Nine are off by one in the count; Ten is Ojas's own position.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Seven persons Ansh, Bani, Hari, Kirat, Meher, Pavitra and Sumer sit around a circular table, equally spaced and all facing the centre.
- Kirat sits second to the right of Ansh.
- Meher sits immediately to the left of Ansh.
- Sumer sits third to the right of Kirat.
- Hari sits between Ansh and Kirat.
- Bani is not an immediate neighbour of Sumer.

How many persons sit between Bani and Meher when counted to the left of Bani?

solution.concept: Facing the centre: the right is anticlockwise, the left clockwise
solution.explanation: Fix Ansh. Going anticlockwise (to the right): Hari (between Ansh and Kirat), Kirat (second to Ansh's right), then two seats, then Sumer (third to Kirat's right), then Meher (immediately to Ansh's left). The two seats between Kirat and Sumer go to Bani and Pavitra; Bani cannot sit next to Sumer, so Bani sits next to Kirat and Pavitra next to Sumer. To Bani's left (clockwise) come Kirat, Hari and Ansh, then Meher: three persons.
steps: Anticlockwise from Ansh: Ansh, Hari, Kirat, _, _, Sumer, Meher
Bani not next to Sumer ⇒ Bani next to Kirat, Pavitra next to Sumer
Clockwise from Bani: Kirat, Hari, Ansh, Meher ⇒ three persons between
solution.why_others_wrong: Four counts Meher too; Two misses one person; counting to Bani's right (Pavitra, Sumer) gives Two as well, which is the wrong direction.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Six persons Akshara, Biren, Dhriti, Elango, Hansika and Jairus sit around a table shaped like an equilateral triangle: three of them at the three corners and three at the middle of the three sides, so corner and side seats alternate. The persons at the corners face away from the centre and those at the middle of the sides face the centre.
- Akshara sits at a corner.
- Biren sits second to the right of Akshara.
- Dhriti sits immediately to the left of Biren.
- Elango sits second to the right of Dhriti.
- Hansika does not sit at a corner.

Who sits second to the left of the person who sits immediately to the right of Hansika?

solution.concept: Right and left depend on the way each seat faces
solution.explanation: Number the seats anticlockwise from Akshara (corner, seat 0); even seats are corners. A person facing the centre has the right anticlockwise; a person facing outside has the right clockwise. Akshara faces outside, so Biren (second to her right) is two seats clockwise: seat 4, a corner. Biren also faces outside, so his left is anticlockwise: Dhriti = seat 5 (a side seat, facing the centre). Elango is second to Dhriti's right (anticlockwise): seat 1. Hansika is not at a corner, so she takes side seat 3 and Jairus corner seat 2. Hansika faces the centre, so immediately to her right (anticlockwise) is seat 4: Biren. Second to Biren's left (anticlockwise, as he faces outside) is seat 0: Akshara.
steps: Akshara 0 (corner, faces out) ⇒ right = clockwise ⇒ Biren = seat 4
Biren faces out ⇒ left = anticlockwise ⇒ Dhriti = 5; Dhriti faces in ⇒ Elango = 5 + 2 = seat 1
Hansika not at a corner ⇒ seat 3; Jairus seat 2
Right of Hansika (faces in) = seat 4 = Biren; second to Biren's left (faces out) = seat 0 = Akshara
solution.why_others_wrong: Jairus and Elango come from treating every person as facing the centre; Dhriti is immediately to Biren's left.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Four married couples sit around a circular table, equally spaced and all facing the centre. The men are Pranjal, Siddhant, Vikram and Yuvan; the women are Bhavika, Diksha, Gayatri and Nandita. Pranjal is married to Bhavika and Siddhant to Diksha; Vikram and Yuvan are married to Gayatri and Nandita, in some order.
- Men and women sit alternately.
- No man sits next to his wife.
- Bhavika sits third to the right of Siddhant.
- Yuvan sits immediately to the left of Diksha.
- Gayatri sits opposite Bhavika.

Who sits opposite Gayatri's husband?

solution.concept: Seating plus a hidden pairing fixed by a 'no spouse adjacent' rule
solution.explanation: Fix Siddhant at seat 0 and count anticlockwise (to the right); men take the even seats and women the odd seats. Bhavika = 3 and Gayatri (opposite) = 7. Diksha is a woman at an odd seat with Yuvan immediately to her left (one seat clockwise); Diksha cannot be at 1 (Yuvan would be on Siddhant's seat 0, and she would sit next to her own husband), so Diksha = 5 and Yuvan = 4. Nandita = 1. Pranjal and Vikram share seats 2 and 6; seat 2 is next to Bhavika, Pranjal's wife, so Pranjal = 6 and Vikram = 2. Vikram sits next to Nandita (seat 1), so Nandita cannot be his wife: Vikram is married to Gayatri, and Yuvan (between Bhavika and Diksha) to Nandita. Opposite Vikram (seat 2) is seat 6: Pranjal.
steps: Siddhant 0; Bhavika 3; Gayatri 7
Yuvan–Diksha: Diksha 1 is impossible (Yuvan on seat 0) ⇒ Diksha 5, Yuvan 4
Nandita 1; Pranjal not next to Bhavika ⇒ Pranjal 6, Vikram 2
Vikram sits next to Nandita ⇒ his wife is Gayatri
Opposite Vikram (2) = seat 6 = Pranjal
solution.why_others_wrong: Siddhant sits opposite Yuvan, who is Nandita's husband; Vikram is Gayatri's husband himself.

steps: Known: R1 M, K5 L, W6 S, T8 L, A9 M
Position 7 between S and L ⇒ M (mediums complete: 1, 7, 9)
Positions 2–4 = one L + two S with no repeats ⇒ S, L, S

C medium ⇒ 7; M ⇒ 4, immediately below K

June → Tejas July → Nalini September works; September would need Nalini in December (Jeet's month), and November would put Tejas in December, Jeet's month. So Arun June, Tejas July, Nalini September. The months between May and December are June to November; nobody travels in August, October and November: three months.

I. T > W
II. T = W

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II is true
Either conclusion I or II is true

solution.concept: Reading a combined inequality chain
solution.explanation: T ≥ U = V ≥ W gives only T ≥ W. T > W and T = W are each uncertain, but together they make up T ≥ W, so one of them must be true: either I or II follows.
steps: T ≥ U = V ≥ W → T ≥ W (no strict sign)
I alone and II alone are not certain
I or II = T ≥ W ⇒ Either I or II follows
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Either' takes the place of 'Both' (four-option rule); T > W and T = W cannot both hold.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Either conclusion I or II is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: M > N = O ≥ P < Q < R

Conclusions:
I. N > P
II. R > P

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II is true
Both conclusions I and II are true

solution.concept: Reading a combined inequality chain
solution.explanation: N = O ≥ P gives only N ≥ P, so N > P is not certain. P < Q < R gives R > P.
steps: I: N = O ≥ P → N ≥ P only → not certain
II: P < Q < R → R > P, true
solution.why_others_wrong: A '≥' path never proves a strict '>'.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Only conclusion II is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Five statements are given: A ≤ B, B = C, C < D, D ≥ E and E > F. Treat all of them as true.

Conclusions:
I. A < D
II. E < C

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II is true
Both conclusions I and II are true

solution.concept: Reading a combined inequality chain
solution.explanation: A ≤ B = C < D gives A < D. C and E lie on opposite sides of the turn at D, so E < C is not certain.
steps: I: A ≤ B = C < D → A < D, true
II: C < D ≥ E: reversal at D → no relation
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only conclusion I is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements: A ♫ B, B ☼ C, C ☾ D, E ♪ D

Conclusions:
I. A ☼ D
II. E ♪ B

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II is true
Both conclusions I and II are true

solution.concept: Decoding worded symbols, then reading the chain
solution.explanation: Decoded: A ≥ B > C = D > E. So A > D (I) and E < B (II): both follow.
steps: A ≥ B, B > C, C = D, E < D ⇒ A ≥ B > C = D > E
I: A > D, true
II: E < B, true
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both conclusions I and II are true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements: F ✿ G, G ♪ H, I ♫ H, I ☾ J

Conclusions:
I. J ☼ F
II. G ♫ I

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II is true
Both conclusions I and II are true

solution.concept: Decoding worded symbols, then reading the chain
solution.explanation: Decoded: F ≤ G < H ≤ I = J. So J > F (I follows). G < I, so 'G ≥ I' is false (II).
steps: Decode: F ≤ G, G < H, I ≥ H, I = J
Chain: F ≤ G < H ≤ I = J
I: J ☼ F means J > F: true
II: G ♫ I means G ≥ I: false
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only conclusion I is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements: K ☼ L, M ♫ L, M ✿ N, O ♪ N

Conclusions:
I. K ☼ M
II. N ♫ L

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II is true
Both conclusions I and II are true

solution.concept: Decoding worded symbols, then reading the chain
solution.explanation: Decoded: K > L ≤ M ≤ N > O. K and M lie on opposite sides of the turn at L, so K > M is not certain. L ≤ M ≤ N gives N ≥ L.
steps: Decode: K > L, M ≥ L, M ≤ N, O < N
Chain: K > L ≤ M ≤ N > O
I: K > M: reversal at L → not certain
II: N ≥ L: true
solution.final_answer: Option B: Only conclusion II is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements: P ☾ Q, Q ♫ R, S ♪ R, S ♫ T

Conclusions:
I. Q ☼ R
II. Q ☾ R

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II is true
Either conclusion I or II is true

solution.concept: Decoding worded symbols, then reading the chain
solution.explanation: Decoded: P = Q ≥ R > S ≥ T. Q ≥ R is given, so Q > R and Q = R are each uncertain, but one of them must be true: either I or II follows.
steps: Decode: P = Q, Q ≥ R, S < R, S ≥ T
Q ≥ R ⇒ (Q > R) or (Q = R)
Either I or II follows
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Either' replaces 'Both' (four-option rule).
solution.final_answer: Option D: Either conclusion I or II is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements: U ♪ V, V ✿ W, X ☼ W, X ✿ Y, Z ♪ Y

Conclusions:
I. Z ♪ W
II. U ☾ V

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II is true
Both conclusions I and II are true

solution.concept: Decoding worded symbols, then reading the chain
solution.explanation: Decoded: U < V ≤ W < X ≤ Y > Z. W and Z lie on opposite sides of the turn at Y, so Z < W is not certain. U < V makes U = V false.
steps: Decode: U < V, V ≤ W, X > W, X ≤ Y, Z < Y
Chain: U < V ≤ W < X ≤ Y > Z
I: Z < W: reversal at Y → not certain
II: U = V: false (U < V)
solution.final_answer: Option C: Neither conclusion I nor II is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: R > S; T ≤ S; U ≥ R; V < T; W = V

Conclusions:
I. U > W
II. R > U

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II is true
Both conclusions I and II are true

solution.concept: Combining five statements into one chain
solution.explanation: Combined: U ≥ R > S ≥ T > V = W. From U down to W every sign points the same way with strict signs on the path, so U > W. R > U contradicts U ≥ R.
steps: Rewrite: U ≥ R, R > S, S ≥ T, T > V, V = W
Chain: U ≥ R > S ≥ T > V = W
I: U > W: true
II: R > U: false (U ≥ R)
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only conclusion I is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: G > H ≥ I; J ≤ I; K = J; L > K

Which of the following conclusions is definitely FALSE?

solution.concept: Definitely false = contradicted by the chain in every case
solution.explanation: Combined: G > H ≥ I ≥ J = K < L. So G > J always, which makes 'J > G' false in every case. H ≥ I ≥ J = K gives only H ≥ K, so H > K may or may not hold. L is above K but cannot be compared with I or H, so L > I and L ≥ H may be true or false.
steps: Chain: G > H ≥ I ≥ J = K < L
J > G: G > J always ⇒ definitely false
H > K: only H ≥ K ⇒ not determined
L > I, L ≥ H: L joins the chain only at K ⇒ not determined
solution.why_others_wrong: The other three are each possible but not certain; 'definitely false' needs a relation that the chain rules out in every case.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: A is the sister of B. B is the son of C. D is the wife of C. How is A related to D?

solution.concept: A sibling of a child is also a child of the same parents
solution.explanation: B is the son of C, and D is C's wife, so D is B's mother. A is B's sister, so A is also D's child: her daughter.
steps: B is C's son; D is C's wife ⇒ D is B's mother
A is B's sister ⇒ A is D's daughter
solution.why_others_wrong: Sister and mother would put A in D's generation or above; niece needs a sibling of D.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Pointing to a man in a photograph, Arif said, "This man's son is my father's only brother." How is the man in the photograph related to Arif?

solution.concept: The father of one's father's brother
solution.explanation: Arif's father's only brother is Arif's paternal uncle. The man in the photograph is the father of that uncle, and brothers share a father, so he is also the father of Arif's father: Arif's grandfather.
steps: My father's only brother = Arif's uncle
The man is that uncle's father
The uncle's father is also Arif's father's father ⇒ grandfather
solution.why_others_wrong: Father would make the man's son Arif's brother; uncle is the man's son, not the man; great-grandfather skips a generation.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: P is the brother of Q. R is the father of P. S is the sister of R. T is the son of S. How is T related to Q?

solution.concept: Children of siblings are cousins
solution.explanation: R is the father of P and therefore also of Q (P and Q are siblings). S is R's sister, so she is Q's aunt, and her son T is Q's cousin.
steps: R is the father of P and Q
S is R's sister ⇒ Q's aunt
S's son T ⇒ Q's cousin
solution.why_others_wrong: Brother would need the same parents as Q; nephew and uncle are one generation off.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: M is the mother-in-law of N, and N is the husband of O. N has only one wife. How is O related to M?

solution.concept: A man's mother-in-law is his wife's mother
solution.explanation: M is N's mother-in-law, so M is the mother of N's wife. N's wife is O, so O is M's daughter.
steps: Mother-in-law of a husband = mother of his wife
N's wife = O ⇒ M is O's mother ⇒ O is M's daughter
solution.why_others_wrong: Daughter-in-law would be the wife of M's son; here M is the mother of N's wife.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Rekha is the wife of Mohan. Mohan's father Gopal has only two children, Mohan and Lata. Ishan is Lata's son. How is Rekha related to Ishan?

solution.concept: The wife of a maternal uncle
solution.explanation: Mohan and Lata are siblings, so Mohan is the brother of Ishan's mother: his maternal uncle. Rekha, Mohan's wife, is therefore Ishan's aunt.
steps: Mohan and Lata are Gopal's two children ⇒ siblings
Lata is Ishan's mother ⇒ Mohan is his maternal uncle
Uncle's wife ⇒ aunt
solution.why_others_wrong: Ishan's mother is Lata; Rekha is in his mother's generation, so she is neither his sister nor his grandmother.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Aunt (wife of his mother's brother)

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability

solution.concept: Decode left to right and keep track of generations
solution.explanation: P is Q's mother; Q is R's brother, so P is R's mother too. R is S's wife, so P is the mother of S's wife: S's mother-in-law.
steps: P ⊡ Q: P is Q's mother
Q ⊠ R: R is Q's sibling ⇒ P is R's mother
R ⊟ S: R is S's wife
Mother of one's wife ⇒ mother-in-law
solution.why_others_wrong: Mother is P's relation to R, not to S; sister-in-law and grandmother put P in the wrong generation.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How is Vimla related to Ria?

solution.concept: Wife of a parent's brother
solution.explanation: Ria's mother is Uma, and Uma's brother is Tarun. Vimla is Tarun's wife, so she is the wife of Ria's maternal uncle: Ria's aunt.
steps: Yash = Uma's husband (Raghav's only daughter) ⇒ Ria's mother = Uma
Tarun = Uma's brother; Vimla = Tarun's wife ⇒ aunt
solution.why_others_wrong: Uma is Ria's mother; Vimla is Uma's sister-in-law, not Ria's; Sushila is Ria's grandmother.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How is Yash related to Tarun?

solution.concept: Sister's husband
solution.explanation: Yash is married to Uma, Tarun's sister, so Yash is Tarun's brother-in-law.
steps: Son-in-law of Raghav ⇒ husband of Raghav's daughter Uma
Uma is Tarun's sister ⇒ brother-in-law
solution.why_others_wrong: Yash is Raghav's son-in-law, not Tarun's; he shares no parent with Tarun.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How is Sushila related to Yash?

solution.concept: Wife's mother
solution.explanation: Yash's wife is Uma, and Sushila is Uma's mother, so Sushila is Yash's mother-in-law.
steps: Yash's wife = Uma
Uma's mother = Sushila ⇒ mother-in-law

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability

solution.concept: Mother's sister's relation to the child
solution.explanation: L is M's son and M is N's husband, so N is L's mother. N is O's sister, so O is L's maternal aunt, and L (a son) is O's nephew.
steps: L ∝ M: L is M's son (male)
M ≈ N: N is M's wife ⇒ L's mother
N ∞ O: O is the sister of L's mother
Son of one's sister ⇒ nephew
solution.why_others_wrong: Son would make O a parent of L; brother and cousin put L in the wrong generation or branch.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Kamla is the mother-in-law of Mohit's mother. Kamla has only one son, Ramesh, who has only one wife, Sunita. Sunita's daughter Pallavi, whose father is Ramesh, is married to Ajay. How is Ajay related to Mohit?

solution.concept: Identify the parents first, then the sibling's spouse
solution.explanation: Kamla's daughter-in-law must be the wife of her only son, Ramesh: Sunita. So Mohit's mother is Sunita and his father Ramesh. Pallavi is the daughter of Ramesh and Sunita, so she is Mohit's sister, and her husband Ajay is Mohit's brother-in-law.
steps: Mother-in-law of Mohit's mother ⇒ Mohit's mother married Kamla's son
Only son Ramesh, only wife Sunita ⇒ Mohit's parents are Ramesh and Sunita
Pallavi = Mohit's sister ⇒ her husband is his brother-in-law
solution.why_others_wrong: Ajay is Ramesh's son-in-law, not Mohit's; he is neither Mohit's brother nor his uncle.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Sameer walks 12 m towards the north. He then turns left and walks 5 m, and then turns left again and walks 7 m. How far is he now from his starting point, and in which direction?

solution.concept: Net displacement
solution.explanation: Left from north is west, and left from west is south. He ends 5 m west and 12 − 7 = 5 m north of the start: √(25 + 25) = 5√2 m, towards the north-west.
steps: 12 m north → (0, 12)
Left = west; 5 m → (−5, 12)
Left = south; 7 m → (−5, 5)
solution.why_others_wrong: North-East takes the first left as east; 13 m uses 12 and 5 as the legs; 5 m, West forgets the remaining northward 5 m.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Point A is 4 m south of point B. Point C is 4 m west of point A. Point D is 6 m north of point C. In which direction is point D with respect to point B?

solution.concept: Place every point on a grid
solution.explanation: Take B at (0, 0). A = (0, −4), C = (−4, −4) and D = (−4, 2). D is 4 m west and 2 m north of B: north-west.
steps: D − B = (−4, +2) ⇒ North-West
solution.why_others_wrong: South-West ignores that D is 2 m north of B; West ignores the north component.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: A girl is facing north-east. She turns 225° clockwise and then 90° anticlockwise. Which direction is she facing now?

solution.concept: Net turn = clockwise − anticlockwise
solution.explanation: The net turn is 225° − 90° = 135° clockwise. Starting from north-east (45°), 45° + 135° = 180°: south.
steps: Net turn: 225° clockwise − 90° = 135° clockwise
North-East = 45° ⇒ 45° + 135° = 180° = South
solution.why_others_wrong: West stops after the first turn; North turns the wrong way; South-West adds only 180°.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the straight-line distance between T and R, and in which direction is R from T?

solution.concept: A 9-12-15 right triangle
solution.explanation: R is 12 km east and 9 km north of T: √(144 + 81) = 15 km, towards the north-east.
steps: Coordinates (east, north) in km with T at (0, 0): T (0, 0), Q (0, 9), R (12, 9), S (12, -5), U (-8, -5), V (-8, 6)
√(12² + 9²) = 15 km; east and north ⇒ North-East
solution.why_others_wrong: 21 km adds the two legs; North-West swaps east for west; 12 km, East ignores the 9 km north.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How far is the drone's landing point V from its starting point T, and in which direction?

solution.concept: Net displacement of the whole route
solution.explanation: V = (−8, 6): 8 km west and 6 km north of T, so √(64 + 36) = 10 km towards the north-west.
steps: Coordinates (east, north) in km with T at (0, 0): T (0, 0), Q (0, 9), R (12, 9), S (12, -5), U (-8, -5), V (-8, 6)
√(8² + 6²) = 10 km; west and north ⇒ North-West
solution.why_others_wrong: North-East takes the 20 km leg as east; 14 km adds 8 and 6; South-West uses the point U.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In which direction is S with respect to U?

solution.concept: Same north coordinate ⇒ a pure east–west direction
solution.explanation: S = (12, −5) and U = (−8, −5) are on the same east–west line, with S 20 km to the east of U.
steps: Coordinates (east, north) in km with T at (0, 0): T (0, 0), Q (0, 9), R (12, 9), S (12, -5), U (-8, -5), V (-8, 6)
S − U = (20, 0) ⇒ East
solution.why_others_wrong: West is U's direction from S; the other two need a north or south difference, which is zero.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which landmark (other than T) is nearest to T in a straight line?

solution.concept: Compare straight-line distances
solution.explanation: Distances from T: Q 9 km, U √89 ≈ 9.4 km, V 10 km, S 13 km, R 15 km. Q is the nearest.
steps: Coordinates (east, north) in km with T at (0, 0): T (0, 0), Q (0, 9), R (12, 9), S (12, -5), U (-8, -5), V (-8, 6)
solution.why_others_wrong: U is a close second (√89 ≈ 9.43 km); V is 10 km and S 13 km away.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: At about 4 pm on a sunny day, Kriti stood beside a lamp post and then walked straight towards the tip of the post's shadow. After reaching the tip, she turned to her left and kept walking. In which direction was she walking then?

solution.concept: Afternoon shadows point east
solution.explanation: In the afternoon the sun is in the west, so shadows point east. Walking towards the tip of the shadow means walking east. A left turn from east is north.
steps: Afternoon: sun in the west ⇒ shadow towards the east
Walking to the tip ⇒ facing east
Left of east ⇒ north
solution.why_others_wrong: South is a right turn from east; West would be walking towards the sun; East ignores the turn.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: A cyclist rides 6 km towards the south, turns right and rides 4 km, turns right again and rides 11 km, and then turns left and rides 8 km. How far is the cyclist from the starting point, and in which direction?

solution.concept: Track the facing direction after each turn
solution.explanation: Right from south is west; right from west is north; left from north is west. Net: west 4 + 8 = 12 km and north 11 − 6 = 5 km. √(144 + 25) = 13 km, towards the north-west.
steps: Right ⇒ west 4 → (−4, −6)
Right ⇒ north 11 → (−4, 5)
Left ⇒ west 8 → (−12, 5)
√(12² + 5²) = 13 km, North-West
solution.why_others_wrong: North-East flips the east–west part; 17 km adds 12 and 5; 12 km, West ignores the 5 km north.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: A wall clock is laid flat on a table so that the hour hand points towards the north when the time is exactly 3 o'clock. At 7:30 the same day, in which direction does the minute hand point?

solution.concept: Rotate the whole dial with the given reference
solution.explanation: At 3 o'clock the hour hand points at the '3', so the '3' faces north. Going clockwise around the dial, '6' is a quarter-turn after '3', so it faces east ('12' faces west and '9' south). At 7:30 the minute hand points at the '6': east.
steps: '3' → north
Clockwise quarter-turns: '6' → east, '9' → south, '12' → west
7:30 ⇒ minute hand at '6' ⇒ east
solution.why_others_wrong: West is where the '12' points; South-West would be between '9' and '12'; North is the '3'.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Anu and Babli stand back to back. Anu faces north-east. Babli then turns 90° clockwise. Which direction does Babli face now?

solution.concept: Back to back = opposite directions
solution.explanation: Standing back to back, Babli faces the opposite of north-east: south-west (225°). A 90° clockwise turn gives 225° + 90° = 315°: north-west.
steps: Back to back ⇒ Babli faces south-west (225°)
solution.why_others_wrong: South-East is a 90° anticlockwise turn; North-East is Anu's direction; South-West ignores the turn.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Ravi and Sita start from the same point X. Ravi walks 10 m north, turns right and walks 6 m, then turns right again and walks 4 m. Sita walks 6 m east, turns left and walks 14 m, then turns left again and walks 15 m. How far is Sita from Ravi now, and in which direction from him?

solution.concept: Put both end points on one grid
solution.explanation: Ravi: north 10, east 6, south 4 ⇒ (6, 6). Sita: east 6, north 14, west 15 ⇒ (−9, 14). Sita is 15 m west and 8 m north of Ravi: √(225 + 64) = 17 m, towards the north-west.
steps: Difference (−15, +8)
√(15² + 8²) = 17 m, North-West
solution.why_others_wrong: South-East is Ravi's direction from Sita; 23 m adds 15 and 8; 15 m, North ignores the west part.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: At 7 am on a clear day, Neha starts from point A and walks 5 km straight towards the sun. She then turns left and walks 12 km, and then turns left again and walks 10 km. How far is she from A, and in which direction?

solution.concept: Fix the first direction from the morning sun
solution.explanation: At 7 am the sun is in the east, so she first walks east 5 km. Left from east is north (12 km), and left from north is west (10 km). Net: 5 km west and 12 km north, so √(25 + 144) = 13 km, towards the north-west.
steps: Morning sun ⇒ first leg east: (5, 0)
Left ⇒ north 12: (5, 12)
Left ⇒ west 10: (−5, 12)
√(5² + 12²) = 13 km, North-West
solution.why_others_wrong: North-East forgets that the 10 km west leg overshoots the start; South-West reverses both parts; 17 km adds 5 and 12.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code language, WINTER is written as XHOSFQ. How is SUMMER written in that code language?

solution.concept: Alternate letters move forward and backward
solution.explanation: W+1 = X, I−1 = H, N+1 = O, T−1 = S, E+1 = F, R−1 = Q: letters in odd places move one step forward and letters in even places one step back. SUMMER: S+1 = T, U−1 = T, M+1 = N, M−1 = L, E+1 = F, R−1 = Q.
steps: SUMMER → TTNLFQ
solution.why_others_wrong: TVNNFS moves every letter forward; RTLLDQ moves every letter back; TTNLFS moves the last letter forward instead of back.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, ACE is written as 15 and BED is written as 40. How is DEAF written in that code?

solution.concept: Product of the alphabet positions
solution.why_others_wrong: 16 is the sum of the positions; 24 leaves out E (4 × 1 × 6); 480 multiplies the product by the number of letters.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code language, 'mango is sweet' is written as 'ta po ki', 'sweet ripe fruit' is written as 'ki lu ra' and 'fruit is fresh' is written as 'ra po ne'. (The codes of the words in a sentence may be in any order.) What is the code for 'mango'?

solution.concept: Remove the codes of the shared words
solution.explanation: 'is' appears in sentences 1 and 3, whose common code is po. 'sweet' appears in sentences 1 and 2, common code ki. Sentence 1 is 'mango is sweet' = 'ta po ki', so mango = ta.
steps: is = po (sentences 1 & 3)
sweet = ki (sentences 1 & 2)
mango = remaining code of sentence 1 = ta
solution.why_others_wrong: po is 'is', ki is 'sweet' and ne is 'fresh'.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, GARDEN is written as MVWIZT. How is PLANET written in that code?

solution.concept: Opposite letters, then reverse
solution.explanation: Replace each letter by its opposite (A↔Z, B↔Y, …): GARDEN → TZIWVM, which reversed is MVWIZT. PLANET → KOZMVG → reversed GVMZOK.
steps: Opposites of GARDEN: T Z I W V M
Reverse: MVWIZT ✓
PLANET → K O Z M V G
Reverse: GVMZOK
solution.why_others_wrong: KOZMVG skips the reversal; GVMZOL takes the opposite of P as L; TENALP only reverses the word.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, 5274 is written as 1436 and 8193 is written as 0728. How is 6385 written in that code?

solution.concept: Swap the digits in pairs, then subtract 1 from each digit
solution.explanation: 5274: swap the 1st–2nd and 3rd–4th digits → 2547, then subtract 1 from every digit → 1436. 8193 → 1839 → 0728. 6385 → 3658 → 2547.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3658 stops after the swap; 5274 subtracts 1 without swapping; 2548 does not reduce the last digit.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, LOAN is written as OANL2 and CREDIT is written as REDITC2. How is SAVINGS written in that code?

solution.concept: Two parts: a letter move and a count
solution.explanation: LOAN → OANL (first letter moved to the end) + 2 (its vowels O, A). CREDIT → REDITC + 2 (E, I). Other counts do not fit both: LOAN has 2 consonants but CREDIT has 4, and the lengths are 4 and 6. SAVINGS → AVINGSS + 2 (A, I).
steps: Move: first letter to the end (LOAN → OANL, CREDIT → REDITC)
Number: vowels (2 in LOAN, 2 in CREDIT); consonant counts 2 and 4 and lengths 4 and 6 do not fit
SAVINGS → AVINGSS, vowels A and I ⇒ AVINGSS2
solution.why_others_wrong: AVINGSS5 counts the consonants; SSAVING2 moves the last letter to the front; AVINGSS7 uses the word length.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which element is 5th to the left of the 8th element from the right end?

solution.explanation: The 8th element from the right is the 15th from the left (L). Five places to its left is the 10th element: T.
steps: 8th from the right = 22 − 8 + 1 = 15th from the left = L

Matches: @ 9, $ 6

questions.question_text: If all the symbols are removed from the arrangement, which element will be 10th from the left end?

solution.concept: Delete first, then count

steps: Remove %, @, #, $, &
New arrangement: K 5 M 2 E 9 R T 3 A 7 L 6 U P 1 W

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How many letters are there between M and U in the arrangement?

Letters among them: E, R, T, A, L

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If all the symbols are removed, which element will be 4th to the right of the 9th element from the right end?

4 places to the right ⇒ 16th = E

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability

Right neighbours: I → 7, O → 5, A → #, E → 6

steps: New order: O H © 2 F ★ Q 7 I 4 £ D 9 5 ¥ S 8 A # 3 E 6 Z @ N 1

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If every letter in an odd-numbered position of the English alphabet (A, C, E, …) is removed, which letter will be 7th from the right end of the remaining letters?

solution.concept: Keep the even-position letters
solution.explanation: The remaining letters are B D F H J L N P R T V X Z (13 letters). Counting from the right: Z, X, V, T, R, P, N.
steps: Remaining: B D F H J L N P R T V X Z
7th from the right = 7th from the left of the reversed list = N
solution.why_others_wrong: L is 8th and P 6th from the right; M was removed (it is 13th, an odd position).

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If every third letter of the English alphabet (C, F, I, …) is removed, which letter will be 10th from the left end of the remaining letters?

solution.concept: Two of every three letters remain
solution.explanation: Remaining letters: A B D E G H J K M N P Q S T V W Y Z. The 10th is N.
steps: Every block of three keeps its first two letters
10th remaining = 2nd letter of the 5th block (M N O) = N
solution.shortcut: Ten remaining letters = five blocks of two; the 5th block is M N O, so the 10th is N.
solution.why_others_wrong: M is the 9th remaining letter; O was removed; P is the 11th.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which of the following words can be formed using the letters of the word 'INTERNATIONAL', each letter used no more often than it appears in INTERNATIONAL?

solution.concept: Compare letter counts

ALTERNATION: A2 E1 I1 L1 N3 O1 R1 T2 ✓
INTERVAL (V), LATITUDE (U, D), TERMINAL (M) ✗

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If the words BANNER, BANK, BANQUET, BANJO and BANDIT are arranged in the order in which they appear in an English dictionary, which word will be third?

solution.concept: Dictionary order is decided by the first letter that differs
solution.explanation: All five start with BAN, so compare the 4th letters: D (BANDIT), J (BANJO), K (BANK), N (BANNER), Q (BANQUET). The third is BANK.
steps: Common prefix BAN
4th letters: D < J < K < N < Q
Order: BANDIT, BANJO, BANK, BANNER, BANQUET
solution.why_others_wrong: BANJO is second, BANNER fourth and BANDIT first.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How many pairs of letters are there in the word 'FLOWCHART' each of which has as many letters between them in the word as in the English alphabet (counting both forward and backward)?

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Each letter of the word 'BLANKET' is replaced by the letter three places after it in the English alphabet, and the new letters are then arranged in alphabetical order from left to right. Which letter will be third from the left?

solution.concept: Transform, then sort
solution.explanation: B→E, L→O, A→D, N→Q, K→N, E→H, T→W gives E O D Q N H W. In alphabetical order: D E H N O Q W. The third is H.
steps: +3: E O D Q N H W
Sorted: D E H N O Q W
3rd = H
solution.why_others_wrong: E is second; N fourth; O fifth.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Rohit ranks 13th from the top in a class of 41 students. What is his rank from the bottom?

solution.concept: From the other end = total − rank + 1
solution.explanation: Rank from the bottom = 41 − 13 + 1 = 29th.
steps: 41 − 13 = 28 students below Rohit
Rank from the bottom = 28 + 1 = 29th
solution.why_others_wrong: 28th forgets to add 1; 30th adds 2; 27th subtracts 1 instead of adding.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a queue, Asha is 5th from the front and Bina, who stands behind Asha, is 6th from the back. Exactly eight persons stand between Asha and Bina. How many persons are there in the queue?

solution.concept: Front part + between + back part
solution.explanation: Asha's position from the front is 5. Eight persons stand between, so Bina is 5 + 8 + 1 = 14th from the front. She is 6th from the back, so the queue has 14 + 6 − 1 = 19 persons.
steps: Bina = 5 + 9 = 14th from the front
solution.why_others_wrong: 18 subtracts one person too many; 20 forgets to subtract Bina once; 21 counts both Asha and Bina twice.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Among five boys A, B, C, D and E, each of a different height, A is taller than B, C is shorter than B, D is taller than A, and E is the shortest. Who is the third tallest?

solution.concept: Build the order from pairwise clues
solution.explanation: D > A > B > C, and E is last: D, A, B, C, E. The third tallest is B.
steps: D > A > B > C
E shortest ⇒ D, A, B, C, E
Third = B
solution.why_others_wrong: A is second, D tallest, C fourth.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Anu is 7th from the left end and 15th from the right end of a row of girls. How many more girls must join the row so that there are 30 girls in it?

solution.concept: Total from both ends
solution.explanation: The row has 7 + 15 − 1 = 21 girls, so 30 − 21 = 9 more are needed.
solution.why_others_wrong: 8 forgets to subtract Anu once (22 girls); 10 subtracts her twice; 7 is her position.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a class of 31 students, 6 students failed an examination and are ranked below all those who passed. Among the students who passed, Ravi is 7th from the top. What is Ravi's rank from the bottom in the whole class?

solution.concept: Failed students sit below him, so they count
solution.explanation: Since everyone who failed is ranked below everyone who passed, Ravi is also 7th from the top of the whole class. His rank from the bottom is 31 − 7 + 1 = 25th.
steps: Failed students are below all passed students ⇒ Ravi is 7th from the top overall
From the bottom: 31 − 7 + 1 = 25
solution.why_others_wrong: 19th is his rank from the bottom among the 25 who passed only; 24th forgets to add 1; 26th adds 2.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Some persons sit in a row, all facing north. Amit is 11th from the left end and Bhola is 16th from the right end. Chetan sits exactly midway between Amit and Bhola, and exactly seven persons sit between Amit and Chetan. How many persons sit in the row?

solution.concept: Midpoint doubles the distance
solution.explanation: Seven persons between Amit and Chetan put Chetan 8 places from Amit. Bhola cannot be to Amit's left (Chetan would be at position 3 and Bhola at −5), so Chetan is 19th and Bhola, as far again, is 27th from the left. With Bhola 16th from the right, the row has 27 + 16 − 1 = 42 persons.
steps: Chetan = 11 + 8 = 19th (the left side is impossible)
Bhola = 19 + 8 = 27th from the left
solution.why_others_wrong: 41 subtracts Bhola twice; 43 forgets to subtract him once; 40 places Chetan 7 places away instead of 8.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Class A has 28 students and class B has 32. In class A, Ritu is 9th from the top; in class B, Sonu is 11th from the bottom. The two classes are combined into one ranking list of 60 students, in which Ritu is 15th from the top and Sonu is 23rd from the bottom. How many students are ranked between Ritu and Sonu in the combined list?

solution.concept: Only the combined-list positions matter
solution.explanation: In the combined list of 60, Ritu is 15th from the top and Sonu is 60 − 23 + 1 = 38th from the top. Between them are 38 − 15 − 1 = 22 students. The ranks within the old classes are not needed.
steps: Sonu from the top = 60 − 23 + 1 = 38th
Between 15th and 38th: 38 − 15 − 1 = 22
solution.why_others_wrong: 21 subtracts one too many; 23 forgets to exclude one end; 40 mixes the class ranks with the combined ranks.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by two statements, I and II. Decide whether the data in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.

Question: What is the straight-line distance between village P and village Q?

I. Village P is 6 km north of village R.
II. Village Q is 8 km east of village R.

options.text: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not sufficient
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not sufficient
Statements I and II together are not sufficient
Both statements I and II together are necessary

solution.concept: Data sufficiency: test each statement alone, then together
solution.explanation: I places P relative to R but says nothing about Q; II places Q relative to R but says nothing about P. Together, P and Q are the ends of a right angle at R with legs 6 km and 8 km, so PQ = 10 km.
steps: I alone: Q unknown ⇒ not sufficient
II alone: P unknown ⇒ not sufficient
Together: √(6² + 8²) = 10 km ⇒ both needed
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both statements I and II together are necessary

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by three statements, I, II and III. Decide which of the statements are sufficient to answer the question.

Question: How many students are there in the class?

I. Ravi is 12th from the top.
II. Sita is 20th from the bottom.
III. Ravi is 4 ranks above Sita.

options.text: Only statements I and III together are sufficient
Only statements II and III together are sufficient
All three statements I, II and III together are necessary
Even all three statements together are not sufficient

solution.concept: Three-statement data sufficiency: test every pair
solution.explanation: To count the class we need one person's rank from both ends. I + III: Sita is 16th from the top, but her rank from the bottom is unknown. II + III: Ravi is 24th from the bottom, but his rank from the top is unknown. I + II: two different persons, with no link between them. All three: Sita is 16th from the top and 20th from the bottom, so the class has 16 + 20 − 1 = 35 students.
steps: I + II: no link between Ravi and Sita ⇒ not sufficient
I + III: Sita 16th from the top only
II + III: Ravi 24th from the bottom only
All three: 16 + 20 − 1 = 35 ⇒ all three needed
solution.final_answer: Option C: All three statements I, II and III together are necessary

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two assumptions. An assumption is something supposed or taken for granted by the person making the statement. Decide which of the assumptions is/are implicit in the statement.

Statement: Notice in a library: "Books must be returned within 14 days. A fine of ₹5 per day will be charged after that."

Assumptions:
I. Some borrowers may keep books for longer than 14 days.
II. The fine will encourage borrowers to return books on time.

options.text: Neither I nor II is implicit
Both I and II are implicit

solution.concept: Implicit assumption: what the speaker must take for granted
solution.explanation: A rule with a late fine is needed only if some borrowers might keep books beyond the limit (I). Fixing a fine assumes that it will push borrowers to return books on time (II); otherwise the fine would serve no purpose.
steps: Late-return rule ⇒ late returns are expected: I implicit

Other expenses unknown ⇒ II does not follow

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Either conclusion I or II follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
In a class of 40 students, every student plays at least one of the two games, cricket and football. 25 students play cricket and 22 play football.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability

Members who completed the programme were very satisfied with it

Weakener: completers were a self-selected group already losing weight

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability

Passage: A city gets all its water from two lakes, A and B. Last year each lake supplied half of the city's water. This year lake A supplied 60% of the water, and the total supply was the same as last year.

options.text: The city's demand for water fell this year
Lake A will supply 70% of the water next year
Lake B supplied less water this year than last year

solution.concept: Shares of an unchanged total
solution.explanation: With the total unchanged, lake B's share fell from 50% to 40%, so it supplied less water than last year.
steps: Total unchanged
Lake B: 50% → 40% of the same total ⇒ less water
solution.why_others_wrong: The passage gives no reason for the change (drying up is a guess); demand is not mentioned and the total supply did not change; next year's share is a prediction.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Lake B supplied less water this year than last year

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Argument: Since the city started a free bus service for women, the number of women travelling by bus has risen by 40%. So the free service has increased the number of trips that women in the city make.

Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

Buses on some routes have become crowded during peak hours
Many men have asked for free bus travel as well
The free service costs the city a large amount every year

solution.concept: Weaken: the evidence shows a shift between modes, not more trips
solution.explanation: The conclusion is about the number of trips, but the evidence is about bus ridership. If the new riders only switched from other modes and total trips are unchanged, the conclusion fails.
steps: Evidence: more women on buses
Conclusion: more trips by women
Weakener: riders switched modes; total trips unchanged
solution.why_others_wrong: Crowding, men's demands and the cost of the scheme do not bear on whether women make more trips.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Most of the new women bus riders earlier made the same trips by auto-rickshaw or shared taxi, and the total number of trips made by women in the city has not changed

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Passage: This year, the total deposits of Bank X rose by 8%. Its current-account deposits rose by 20%, and all its other deposits together rose by 5%.

Which of the following must be true?

options.text: This year, current-account deposits are larger than all other deposits together
Last year, current-account deposits made up exactly 20% of the bank's total deposits
The bank's other deposits fell this year
The share of current-account deposits in total deposits fell this year

solution.concept: Weighted average of two growth rates
solution.explanation: Let last year's current-account deposits be C and other deposits O. Then 0.20C + 0.05O = 0.08(C + O), so 0.12C = 0.03O and O = 4C. Current-account deposits were C ÷ 5C = 20% of the total.
steps: Share last year = C / (C + 4C) = 20%
solution.why_others_wrong: This year current deposits are 1.2C against 4.2C of others; other deposits rose by 5%; the current-account share rose (it grew faster than the total).
solution.final_answer: Option B: Last year, current-account deposits made up exactly 20% of the bank's total deposits

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability

steps: Problem 1: ineligible names
Problem 2: needy families excluded
Remedy: verify, remove and enrol — the scheme continues for genuine holders
solution.why_others_wrong: Stopping the scheme or cancelling all cards punishes genuine beneficiaries; doing nothing leaves both problems in place.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Verify the list door to door, remove ineligible names and enrol the needy families who were left out

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
